\section*{Question 5}

Let \(g\) be a continuous function with \(g(2)=5\). The graph of the piecewise-linear function \(g^{\prime}\), the derivative of \(g\), is shown above for \(-3 \leq x \leq 7\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Find the \(x\)-coordinate of all points of inflection of the graph of \(y=g(x)\) for \(-3<x<7\). Justify your answer.
\item[(b)] Find the absolute maximum value of \(g\) on the interval \(-3 \leq x \leq 7\). Justify your answer.
\item[(c)] Find the average rate of change of \(g(x)\) on the interval \(-3 \leq x \leq 7\).
\item[(d)] Find the average rate of change of \(g^{\prime}(x)\) on the interval \(-3 \leq x \leq 7\). Does the Mean Value Theorem applied on the interval \(-3 \leq x \leq 7\) guarantee a value of \(c\), for \(-3<c<7\), such that \(g^{\prime \prime}(c)\) is equal to this average rate of change? Why or why not?
\item[(a)] \(g^{\prime}\) changes from increasing to decreasing at \(x=1\); \(g^{\prime}\) changes from decreasing to increasing at \(x=4\).
Points of inflection for the graph of \(y=g(x)\) occur at \(x=1\) and \(x=4\).
\item[(b)] The only sign change of \(g^{\prime}\) from positive to negative in the interval is at \(x=2\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
g(-3) & =5+\int_{2}^{-3} g^{\prime}(x) d x=5+\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)+4=\frac{15}{2} \\
g(2) & =5 \\
g(7) & =5+\int_{2}^{7} g^{\prime}(x) d x=5+(-4)+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
The maximum value of \(g\) for \(-3 \leq x \leq 7\) is \(\frac{15}{2}\).
\item[(c)] \(\frac{g(7)-g(-3)}{7-(-3)}=\frac{\frac{3}{2}-\frac{15}{2}}{10}=-\frac{3}{5}\)
\item[(d)] \(\frac{g^{\prime}(7)-g^{\prime}(-3)}{7-(-3)}=\frac{1-(-4)}{10}=\frac{1}{2}\)
\end{itemize}

No, the MVT does not guarantee the existence of a
